transcript.text: Hello, Tourist Information Centre, Mike speaking, how can I help you?
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Oh, hi.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I wanted to find out about cookery classes.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I believe there are some one-day classes for tourists?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, they’re open to everyone, but tourists are always welcome.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: OK, let me give you some details of what’s available.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: There are several classes.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: One very popular one is at the Food Studio.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: OK
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: They focus on seasonal products, and as well as teaching you how to cook them, they also show you how to choose them.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Right, that sounds good.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: How big are the classes?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’m not sure exactly, but they’ll be quite small.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: And could I get a private lesson there?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I think so … let me check, yes, they do offer those.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Though in fact most of the people who attend the classes find it’s a nice way of getting to know one another.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: I suppose it must be, yes.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: And this company has a special deal for clients where they offer a discount of 20 percent if you return for a further class.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: But you said there were several classes?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Another one you might be interested in is Bond’s Cookery School.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: They’re quite new, they just opened six months ago, but I’ve heard good things about them.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: They concentrate on teaching you to prepare healthy food, and they have quite a lot of specialist staff.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: So is that food for people on a diet and things like that?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I don’t know if I’d be interested in that.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I don’t think they particularly focus on low calorie diets or weight loss.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: It’s more to do with recipes that look at specific needs, like including ingredients that will help build up your bones and make them stronger, that sort of thing.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I might be interested, I’m not sure.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Do they have a website I could check?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, just key in the name of the school – it’ll come up.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: And if you want to know more about them, every Thursday evening they have a lecture at the school.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: It’s free and you don’t need to book or anything, just turn up at 7.30.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: And that might give you an idea of whether you want to go to an actual class.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: OK, there’s one more place you might be interested in.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: That’s got a rather strange name, it’s called The Arretsa Centre – that’s spelled A-R-R-E-T-S-A.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: They’ve got a very good reputation.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: They do a bit of meat and fish cookery but they mostly specialise in vegetarian dishes.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s certainly an area I’d like to learn more about.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’ve got lots of friends who don’t eat meat.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: In fact, I think I might have seen that school today.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Is it just by the market?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: So they don’t have any problem getting their ingredients.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: They’re right next door.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: And they also offer a special two-hour course in how to use a knife.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: They cover all the different skills – buying them, sharpening, chopping techniques.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: It gets booked up quickly though so you’d need to check it was available.
transcript.speaker: OFFICIAL

transcript.text: Right, well thank you very much.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’ll go and …
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Good evening everyone.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: My name’s Phil Sutton, and I’m chairman of the Highways Committee.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve called this meeting to inform members of the public about the new regulations for traffic and parking we’re proposing for Granford.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’ll start by summarising these changes before we open the meeting to questions.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So, why do we need to make these changes to traffic systems in Granford?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Well, we’re very aware that traffic is becoming an increasing problem.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s been especially noticeable with the increase in heavy traffic while they’ve been building the new hospital.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But it’s the overall rise in the volume of traffic of all kinds that’s concerning us.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: To date there’s not been any increase in traffic accidents, but that’s not something we want to see happen, obviously.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We recently carried out a survey of local residents, and their responses were interesting.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: People were very concerned about the lack of visibility on some roads due to cars parked along the sides of the roads.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’d expected complaints about the congestion near the school when parents are dropping off their children or picking them up, but this wasn’t top of the list, and nor were noise and fumes from trucks and lorries, though they were mentioned by some people.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We think these new traffic regulations would make a lot of difference.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But we still have a long way to go.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve managed to keep our proposals within budget, just, so they can be covered by the Council.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But, of course, it’s no good introducing new regulations if we don’t have a way of making sure that everyone obeys them, and that’s an area we’re still working on with the help of representatives from the police force.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, so this slide shows a map of the central area of Granford, with the High Street in the middle and School Road on the right.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, we already have a set of traffic lights in the High Street at the junction with Station Road, but we’re planning to have another set at the other end, at the School Road junction, to regulate the flow or traffic along the High Street.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re decided we definitely need a pedestrian crossing.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We considered putting this on School Road, just outside the school, but in the end we decided that could lead to a lot of traffic congestion so we decided to locate it on the High Street, crossing the road in front of the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s a very busy area, so it should help things there.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re proposing some changes to parking.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: At present, parking isn’t allowed on the High Street outside the library, but we’re going to change that, and allow parking there, but not at the other end of the High Street near School Road.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’ll be a new ‘No Parking’ sign on School Road, just by the entrance to the school, forbidding parking for 25 metres.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This should improve visibility for drivers and pedestrians, especially on the bend just to the north of the school.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As far as disabled drivers are concerned, at present they have parking outside the supermarket, but lorries also use those spaces, so we’ve got two new disabled parking spaces on the side road up towards the bank.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s not ideal, but probably better than the present arrangement.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We also plan to widen the pavement on School Road.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We think we can manage to get an extra half-metre on the bend just before you get to the school, on the same side of the road.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Finally, we’ve introduced new restrictions on loading and unloading for the supermarket, so lorries will only be allowed to stop there before 8 am.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s the supermarket on School Road – we kept to the existing arrangements with the High Street supermarket.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So that’s about it.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, would anyone …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve got to choose a topic for our experiment, haven’t we, Jack?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Were you thinking of something to do with seeds?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I thought we could look at seed germination – how a seed begins to grow.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Any particular reason?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: I know you’re hoping to work in plant science eventually …
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Yeah, but practically everything we do is going to feed into that.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: No, there’s an optional module on seed structure and function in the third year that I might do, so I thought it might be useful for that.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: If I choose that option, I don’t have to do a dissertation module.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Well, I thought for this experiment we could look at the relationship between seed size and the way the seeds are planted.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So, we could plant different sized seeds in different ways, and see which grow best.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: We’d need to allow time for the seeds to come up.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: That should be fine if we start now.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: A lot of the other possible experiments need quite a bit longer.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So that’d make it a good one to choose.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: And I don’t suppose it’d need much equipment; we’re not doing chemical analysis or anything.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Though that’s not really an issue, we’ve got plenty of equipment in the laboratory.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: We need to have a word with the tutor if we’re going to go ahead with it though.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I’m sure our aim’s OK.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: It’s not very ambitious but the assignment’s only ten percent of our final mark, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: But we need to be sure we’re the only ones doing it.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Yeah, it’s only five percent actually, but it’d be a bit boring if everyone was doing it.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Did you read that book on seed germination on our reading list?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: The one by Graves?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: I looked through it for my last experiment, though it wasn’t all that relevant there.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: It would be for this experiment, though.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: I found it quite hard to follow – lots about the theory, which I hadn’t expected
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Yes, I’d been hoping for something more practical.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: It does include references to the recent findings on genetically-modified seeds, though.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Yes, that was interesting.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: I read an article about seed germination by Lee Hall.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: About seeds that lie in the ground for ages and only germinate after a fire?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: That’s the one.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I knew a bit about it already, but not about this research.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: His analysis of figures comparing the times of the fires and the proportion of seeds that germinated was done in a lot of detail – very impressive.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Was that the article with the illustrations of early stages of plant development?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: They were very clear.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: I think those diagrams were in another article.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Anyway, shall we have a look at the procedure for our experiment?
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: We’ll need to get going with it quite soon.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So the first thing we have to do is find our seeds.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think vegetable seeds would be best.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: And obviously they mustn’t all be the same size.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So, how many sorts do we need?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: About four different ones?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think that would be enough.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: There’ll be quite a large number of seeds for each one.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Then, for each seed we need to find out how much it weighs, and also measure its dimensions, and we need to keep a careful record of all that.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: That’ll be quite time-consuming.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: And we also need to decide how deep we’re going to plant the seeds – right on the surface, a few millimetres down, or several centimetres.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So then we get planting.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Do you think we can plant several seeds together in the same plant pot?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: No, I think we need a different one for each seed.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: And we’ll need to label them – we can use different coloured labels.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Then we wait for the seeds to germinate – I reckon that’ll be about three weeks, depending on what the weather’s like.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Then we see if our plants have come up, and write down how tall they’ve grown.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Then all we have to do is look at our numbers, and see if there’s any relation between them.
transcript.speaker: EMMA

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: So …
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Hi.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Today we’re going to be looking at animals in urban environments and I’m going to be telling you about some research on how they’re affected by these environments.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now, in evolutionary terms, urban environments represent huge upheavals, the sorts of massive changes that usually happen over millions of years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And we used to think that only a few species could adapt to this new environment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One species which is well known as being highly adaptable is the crow, and there’ve been various studies about how they manage to learn new skills.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another successful species is the pigeon, because they’re able to perch on ledges on the walls of city buildings, just like they once perched on cliffs by the sea.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But in fact, we’re now finding that these early immigrants were just the start of a more general movement of animals into cities, and of adaptation by these animals to city life.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And one thing that researchers are finding especially interesting is the speed with which they’re doing this – we’re not talking about gradual evolution here – these animals are changing fast.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Let me tell you about some of the studies that have been carried out in this area.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, in the University of Minnesota, a biologist called Emilie Snell-Rood and her colleagues looked at specimens of urbanised small mammals such as mice and gophers that had been collected in Minnesota, and that are now kept in museums there.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And she looked at specimens that had been collected over the last hundred years, which is a very short time in evolutionary terms.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And she found that during that time, these small mammals had experienced a jump in brain size when compared to rural mammals.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now, we can’t be sure this means they’re more intelligent, but since the sizes of other parts of the body didn’t change, it does suggest that something cognitive was going on.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And Snell-Rood thinks that this change might reflect the cognitive demands of adjusting to city life – having to look in different places to find food, for example, and coping with a whole new set of dangers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Then over in Germany at the Max Planck Institute, there’s another biologist called Catarina Miranda who’s done some experiments with blackbirds living in urban and rural areas.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And she’s been looking not at their anatomy but at their behaviour.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So as you might expect, she’s found that the urban blackbirds tend to be quite bold – they’re prepared to face up to a lot of threats that would frighten away their country counterparts.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But there’s one type of situation that does seem to frighten the urban blackbirds, and that’s anything new – anything they haven’t experienced before.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And if you think about it, that’s quite sensible for a bird living in the city.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Jonathan Atwell, in Indiana University, is looking at how a range of animals respond to urban environments.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He’s found that when they’re under stress, their endocrine systems react by reducing the amount of hormones such as corticosterone into their blood.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s a sensible-seeming adaptation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A rat that gets scared every time a subway train rolls past won’t be very successful.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There’s just one more study I’d like to mention which is by Sarah Partan and her team, and they’ve been looking at how squirrels communicate in an urban environment, and they’ve found that a routine part of their communication is carried out by waving their tails.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: You do also see this in the country, but it’s much more prevalent in cities, possibly because it’s effective in a noisy environment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So what are the long-term implications of this?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One possibility is that we may see completely new species developing in cities.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But on the other hand, it’s possible that not all of these adaptations will be permanent.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Once the animal’s got accustomed to its new environment, it may no longer need the features it’s developed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, now we’ve had a look…
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
